tagline.text: A man's eternal declaration of love, built on a hill above Cebu

children.text: A Greco-Roman-style temple built on the Busay hills north of Cebu City by a businessman in memory of his late wife. With Cebu City and the sea visible below its grand columns and statues, it's a hugely popular photo spot, and pairs well with Tops Lookout and Sirao Garden for a half-day trip.
Temple of Leah is a massive neoclassical structure standing about
10km
north of downtown Cebu, midway up the Busay hills at an elevation of several hundred meters. Cebuano businessman Teodorico Soriano Adarna began construction in

in memory of his wife of 53 years, Leah Villa Albino-Adarna, and it's often called the 'Taj Mahal of Cebu.' It was designed with 24 rooms symbolizing their married life, and is still an unfinished structure with some construction ongoing.

As you enter the temple, the first things you notice are the front staircase lined with Corinthian columns, lion statues, and statues in the style of Greek mythology. In the central hall stands a large bronze statue depicting Mrs. Leah, and further inside are spaces displaying the couple's collection and family history. Gold accents and marble-like finishes decorate the building throughout, so photos from any angle look like they were taken on a European trip.

Another appeal of Temple of Leah is the view. Standing on the temple terrace, Cebu City's high-rises, Mactan Island, and the sea beyond all fit into one frame, and on clear days you can even see the horizon toward Bohol. Go in the late afternoon and sunset light streams between the temple's columns; after dark, you can see the illuminated temple together with the city's night lights.

It's not a historic site, but it's a place where you can feel modern Cebuano culture and the family-centered sentiment of Filipinos. It suits couples, travelers who love photography, and families with half a day free in Cebu City, and pairing it with other Busay hills attractions makes for a full afternoon itinerary.

blocks.title: Photos at the grand front staircase

children.text: The most iconic photo spot, where the wide front staircase, columns, and lion statues all fit in one frame. Shoot slightly upward from the bottom of the stairs to capture the building's grandeur.

blocks.title: See the bronze statue of Leah

children.text: The bronze statue of Mrs. Leah standing in the central hall is the very reason the temple was built. Reading the dedication plaque near the entrance changes how the building feels.

blocks.title: View of Cebu City from the terrace

children.text: From the terraces at the back and sides of the temple, you can look down over Cebu City and the Mactan Channel. The breeze is cool, making it a good spot to rest even at midday.
Between
3:30 PM and 5:30 PM
, as the sunlight comes in at an angle, long shadows fall across the gold accents and columns, giving the best photo atmosphere.

After sunset, the illuminated temple has a completely different atmosphere from daytime. However, operating hours have been adjusted recently, so check the official Facebook page before an evening visit.

blocks.title: Combine with other Busay hills sights

children.text: Tops Lookout, Sirao Flower Garden, and scenic cafes around Busay are all within
10–20 minutes
by car, making it easy to continue on a half-day driving route.

Temple of Leah announced that it would shorten its operating hours from
April 6, 2026

, and the new schedule has not been published as a fixed timetable. If it closes early in the late afternoon, leave town a little earlier to see Temple of Leah first and save the Sirao Flower Garden and Tops Lookout for later.
Depart downtown → tour Temple of Leah for
1 hour
→ return downtown. This also works with spare time before heading to the airport, but factor in traffic.
Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB) is the closest. There are daily direct flights from Korea, and it takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
from Manila. From the airport to Temple of Leah takes about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
by car depending on traffic.
This is the most practical option. From central Cebu City (IT Park, Ayala), it takes about
30–40 minutes
by Grab or taxi, about

one way. It's hard to catch a ride back near the temple, so it's better to negotiate a waiting fee with the driver and charter a round trip or a tour of several sights. A half-day charter touring multiple Busay hills spots runs about
To go cheaply, take a jeepney or taxi to around JY Square Mall (Lahug), then take a habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) up the hill. Negotiate about
per person one way, and ask for a helmet, since the road is steep. There is also a jeepney route toward Busay, but it is hard for first-time visitors to work out.
During the dry season from
December
to
May

, clear skies let you see the farthest across the city view. Being on a hill, the temperature is 1–3°C lower than downtown and there's a breeze, making it relatively pleasant even at midday. During the rainy season, June–
November
, afternoon showers and mist often cloud the view, so a morning visit is advantageous.
During the third week of
January

's Sinulog Festival, the Easter holidays, and the Christmas season, many local families visit, making weekend afternoons very crowded. To take photos at leisure, aim for weekday mornings or right after opening.

There is almost no accommodation around Temple of Leah, so it's common to stay in Cebu City and visit as a day trip. The closest lodging areas are IT Park and Lahug, around
30 minutes
by car, with business hotels running about
a night. In the Busay hills there are a few campsites and small lodge-style accommodations with good views, used by travelers who want to enjoy the night view for longer.

Inside the temple there's a simple cafe and snack stand. For a proper meal, use the scenic restaurants and cafes along the Busay hills road, where you can enjoy Filipino grilled dishes and home-style food like sisig and caldereta together with the city night view. Returning downtown to have dinner at a lechon shop around Lahug or at Larsian barbecue alley is also a good way to finish the day.
Entrance fees are often cash-only and change may be limited, so prepare
and
bills.
Operating hours were long known to be
6:00 AM to 11:00 PM
, but a notice of shortened hours was issued in
. Check the official Facebook page before visiting.
Grab is easy to catch going up, but hard to get for the trip back down. Arrange a round-trip charter or agree on a return ride in advance.
The most popular photo spots are the bottom of the front staircase, in front of the central bronze statue, and the side terrace railing. You may need to queue on weekend afternoons.
Using a tripod, drone photography, or commercial shoots (such as wedding snaps) may require separate permission or a fee, so ask at the ticket booth.
The stairs and floors are polished and slippery after rain. Wear shoes with sturdy soles.
The wind can pick up on the hilltop at dusk, so it's good to bring a light jacket.
The road up into the Busay hills has many steep grades and sharp curves. When riding a habal-habal, ask for a helmet and request that the driver not speed.
Some areas of the temple are still under construction, so don't cross the barrier lines.
Climbing onto or leaning against statues and decorations for photos is prohibited.
If you come down late at night, transport may no longer be running, so be sure to secure a way home.
The Busay hills are prone to landslides. During Typhoon Paeng in
October 2022
, a landslide in nearby Sitio Garahe led to the area around Temple of Leah being designated a danger zone, so postpone hill visits on days with heavy rain or typhoon warnings.
Temple of Leah is private property. Operating hours, fees, and photography rules can change without notice, so check the latest announcements.
